scenes.visual: COLOR MAP (both films, and match the figure dna-ladder-parts.webp if its base colours differ, then keep them identical in both films): old strands and their backbones GREY, new strands GOLD, base A RED, base T BLUE, base C GREEN, base G PURPLE, labels WHITE on dark navy. Every strand is drawn as a backbone with an ARROWHEAD at one end. Bases are labelled rectangular blocks with their letter; no molecular structures. Same colour map as the first film. Title card: Inside the Fork. A grey ladder opens into a Y behind the title.

scenes.tts: In the first film, each old strand fixed its new partner. But how does a cell actually build those two new strands, one letter at a time? A real cell does not open the whole molecule at once.
scenes.visual: Open on the last image of the first film: two molecules, each GREY plus GOLD. Rewind it to one GREY ladder. Instead of unzipping all at once, only the left end opens into a Y shape.
scenes.narration: In the first film, each old strand fixed its new partner. But how does a cell actually build those two new strands, one letter at a time? A real cell does not open the whole molecule at once.

scenes.tts: It opens the D N A at a moving Y, called the fork. The fork moves along, opening fresh template as it goes. Both old strands carry arrowheads, and they point opposite ways.
scenes.caption: It opens the DNA at a moving Y, called the fork. The fork moves along, opening fresh template as it goes. Both old strands carry arrowheads, and they point opposite ways.
scenes.visual: Label the Y: fork. The fork slides steadily from left to right, the open arms lengthening. ARROWHEADS on the two GREY templates: the upper template points LEFT, the lower template points RIGHT. A small arrow under the fork reads fork moves. Keep the fork moving slowly in every scene until s09.
scenes.narration: It opens the DNA at a moving Y, called the fork. The fork moves along, opening fresh template as it goes. Both old strands carry arrowheads, and they point opposite ways.

scenes.tts: The enzyme that builds new D N A is D N A polymerase. At each base, it picks the nucleotide that pairs with it. A wrong one almost never gets in. Then it joins that nucleotide to the growing strand with a covalent bond.
scenes.caption: The enzyme that builds new DNA is DNA polymerase. At each base, it picks the nucleotide that pairs with it. A wrong one almost never gets in. Then it joins that nucleotide to the growing strand with a covalent bond.
scenes.visual: A rounded orange-outlined shape labelled DNA polymerase sits on the upper template. Coloured free nucleotides drift nearby; one matching block enters the shape, clicks onto a short GOLD strand, and a white flash marks the covalent bond.
scenes.narration: The enzyme that builds new DNA is DNA polymerase. At each base, it picks the nucleotide that pairs with it. A wrong one almost never gets in. Then it joins that nucleotide to the growing strand with a covalent bond.

scenes.tts: Polymerase has one strict habit. It adds nucleotides only at the arrowhead end of a new strand. So every new strand grows arrowhead first, pointing the opposite way to its template.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the GOLD new strand: its ARROWHEAD glows. Nucleotides attach only at the arrowhead; a nucleotide that tries the tail end bounces off with a small X. A rule banner: adds only at the arrowhead. The new GOLD strand points RIGHT, opposite to its LEFT-pointing GREY template.
scenes.narration: Polymerase has one strict habit. It adds nucleotides only at the arrowhead end of a new strand. So every new strand grows arrowhead first, pointing the opposite way to its template.

scenes.tts: On the upper template, the new strand's arrowhead points the way the fork moves. So polymerase simply follows the fork, adding nucleotide after nucleotide in one long run.
scenes.visual: Zoom out to the whole fork. On the upper arm the GOLD strand lengthens continuously right behind the moving fork, polymerase riding along. A counter in the corner reads: upper strand, 1 piece.
scenes.narration: On the upper template, the new strand's arrowhead points the way the fork moves. So polymerase simply follows the fork, adding nucleotide after nucleotide in one long run.

scenes.tts: Now look at the lower template. Its new strand must point the other way, back away from the fork. If polymerase only adds at the arrowhead, how can it copy this strand?
scenes.visual: Freeze the fork. Spotlight the lower GREY arm, which points RIGHT. A ghost GOLD outline shows the new strand would have to point LEFT, away from the fork. A question mark sits on the lower arm.
scenes.narration: Now look at the lower template. Its new strand must point the other way, back away from the fork. If polymerase only adds at the arrowhead, how can it copy this strand?

scenes.visual: Hold the frozen fork and the ghost outline on the lower arm. Pulse the question mark. Do not show any pieces.

scenes.tts: It builds in short pieces, because the fork opens only a little template at a time. Each piece starts near the fork and grows away from it. When the fork opens more template, a fresh piece starts near the fork and grows back toward the last one. Another enzyme joins the pieces into one strand.
scenes.visual: Unfreeze the fork. On the lower arm a short GOLD piece starts at the fork and grows LEFT, away from it, to the edge of the opened stretch. The fork moves on, opening more template; a new short GOLD piece starts near the fork and grows LEFT until it meets the first. A small grey clip shape labelled enzyme joins them with a flash. Repeat once more. Counter: lower strand pieces 1, 2, 3, then joined.
scenes.narration: It builds in short pieces, because the fork opens only a little template at a time. Each piece starts near the fork and grows away from it. When the fork opens more template, a fresh piece starts near the fork and grows back toward the last one. Another enzyme joins the pieces into one strand.

scenes.tts: Now zoom in on one step, because copying must also be accurate. Polymerase tests each incoming nucleotide against the template. A nucleotide that does not pair is usually turned away.
scenes.visual: Close-up inside the polymerase shape at the upper strand. A wrong block (RED A opposite a GREEN C) tries to enter; edges clash and it is pushed out with a small X. The correct PURPLE G clicks in. A tally panel on the right starts: 1. matching check.
scenes.narration: Now zoom in on one step, because copying must also be accurate. Polymerase tests each incoming nucleotide against the template. A nucleotide that does not pair is usually turned away.

scenes.tts: Sometimes a wrong base slips in anyway. Polymerase checks each new base and removes most wrong ones. This step is called proofreading. Repair enzymes then catch many of the mistakes that slip past.
scenes.visual: A wrong RED A block does click in opposite a GREEN C. Polymerase backs up one step, removes the A, and adds a PURPLE G. Tally adds: 2. proofreading. Then, behind the fork, one leftover mismatch on a finished stretch is spotted by a small wrench-shaped repair enzyme and fixed. Tally adds: 3. repair.
scenes.narration: Sometimes a wrong base slips in anyway. Polymerase checks each new base and removes most wrong ones. This step is called proofreading. Repair enzymes then catch many of the mistakes that slip past.

scenes.tts: Put the checks together: the matching check, proofreading, then repair. Each later check catches many mistakes the earlier ones missed. A textbook estimate is about one uncorrected mistake for every billion bases copied.
scenes.visual: The three tally lines stack into one bar. On screen only: about 1 uncorrected mistake per 1,000,000,000 bases copied (textbook estimate). Show no further calculation.
scenes.narration: Put the checks together: the matching check, proofreading, then repair. Each later check catches many mistakes the earlier ones missed. A textbook estimate is about one uncorrected mistake for every billion bases copied.

scenes.tts: So copying has two jobs. Pairing makes the copy possible, because it tells polymerase which base goes where. Checking makes the copy accurate, because it removes almost every slip.
scenes.visual: Split the frame. Left panel: the rule banner A with T, C with G, labelled possible. Right panel: the three-step tally, labelled accurate. Both panels slide together under the moving fork, then clear before the end card.
scenes.narration: So copying has two jobs. Pairing makes the copy possible, because it tells polymerase which base goes where. Checking makes the copy accurate, because it removes almost every slip.

scenes.visual: Clear the frame. End card with one centered line only, no title and no second line: 'Pairing makes the copy possible; checking makes it accurate.'
